blocks.text: Functions are fundamental in mathematics: they describe how an output depends on an input through a rule of correspondence. To study the different types of functions (one-to-one, onto and bijective) we first need the key ideas of domain, co-domain and range. Graphs of functions help us find intersecting points: where a linear function meets the coordinate axes, where two linear functions intersect, and where a linear and a quadratic function cross. These intersections let us solve equations visually. The unit also explores the graphs of the square root and cube root functions and their special properties. By combining algebraic and graphical methods, this unit builds your problem-solving skills.

blocks.title: About this unit
blocks.text:
What this unit is about: almost every formula you use (area of a square, cost of petrol, distance travelled) is a rule that takes one quantity and gives another. Unit 2 makes this idea exact and teaches you to work with it in algebra and on graphs.
What you will learn: what a function is; domain, co-domain and range; the notation \(f(x)\) and how to find values; the vertical line test; one-to-one, onto, bijective and piecewise functions; intersection points of lines and parabolas found graphically; graphs of \(y = \sqrt{x}\) and \(y = \sqrt[3]{x}\); and real-life growth and decay.
What you need: substituting numbers into expressions, expanding brackets, solving linear and quadratic equations, and plotting points on the \(xy\)-plane.
The term function was introduced by the German mathematician Leibniz (1646-1716) to describe how one quantity depends on another. The following examples show how the term is used:

items: (i) The area \(A\) of a square depends on one of its sides \(x\) by the formula \(A = x^{2}\), so we say that \(A\) is a function of \(x\).
(ii) The volume \(V\) of a sphere depends on its radius \(r\) by the formula \(V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3}\), so we say that \(V\) is a function of \(r\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
In each formula one quantity is chosen freely (the input) and the other is then fixed (the output).
Square: side \(x = 3\) gives area \(A = 3^{2} = 9\). There is no way a square of side 3 could have any other area.
Sphere: radius \(r = 3\) gives \(V = \frac{4}{3}\pi (3)^{3} = 36\pi\). Again exactly one answer.
The words "is a function of" always mean: once the input is known, the output is completely decided.
A function is a rule or correspondence relating two sets in such a way that each element in the first set corresponds to one and only one element in the second set.
Thus in (i) above, a square of a given side has only one area, and in (ii) above, a sphere of a given radius has only one volume.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The definition has two conditions on every element of the first set:
1. it must be connected to some element of the second set (no input is left out), and
2. it must be connected to only one element (no input gets two answers).
Everyday example: every student of a class has exactly one roll number, so "student \(\to\) roll number" is a function. But "person \(\to\) mobile number" is usually not a function, because one person may have two numbers, and a small child may have none.
It is allowed that two different inputs give the same output: two squares can never have the same side and different areas, but two students may have the same height. "Student \(\to\) height" is still a function.
Now we have a formal definition (see 2.1.1 Definition).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. A function is a rule that gives each input exactly one output.
2. "\(A\) is a function of \(x\)" means \(A\) depends on \(x\) and is fixed once \(x\) is known.
3. Every element of the first set must be used, and must get only one partner.
4. Different inputs may share the same output; one input may never have two outputs.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Thinking a function needs different outputs for different inputs. That is a special kind (one-to-one, in 2.1.4); an ordinary function only forbids two outputs for one input.
2. Forgetting that every element of the first set must have a partner. If some input has no output, the rule is not a function on that set.
